Course Schedule
Note: Themes, content, and assigned readings may be adjusted depending on students’ interests and the progress of the course.
Session 1: What Are the “Language Practices” of “Children across Borders”?
After introducing the concept of “children across borders” (Kawakami, 2011), we will examine what kinds of “mobility” children experience in an age of global movement and what kinds of “language practices” they engage in. We will also explore what “literacy” means by reflecting on case studies of children across borders as well as on our own practices.
Session 2: How Have the Language Abilities of “Children across Borders” Been Understood?
We will examine how the language abilities of children growing up in a multilingual context have been conceptualized through major theoretical frameworks. Through various case studies, we will also consider the challenges that children across borders face in school contexts.
Session 3: In What Ways Can We Understand the Plurilingual Competence of “Children across Borders”?
We will introduce theoretical perspectives for understanding the plurilingual competence of children across borders. Through reflection on students’ own experiences and case studies, we will explore linguistic plurality within individuals and language practices that move between languages.
Session 4: What Forms of Instruction and Support Are Provided for Children Learning a Second Language?
We will examine educational practices designed to support children learning Japanese as a second language in Japan and those learning English as a second language in English-speaking contexts. We will consider the challenges and key considerations involved in such practices.
Session 5: What Is Literacy? — Viewing the Language of “Children across Borders” as Sociocultural Practice
We will introduce theoretical perspectives that conceptualize the language and literacy of children across borders as sociocultural practices. We will consider which aspects should be foregrounded when examining their literacy.
Session 6: How Can We Foster the Plurilingual Competence of “Children across Borders”? — A Translanguaging Perspective
Through an introduction to Translanguaging theory and examples of educational practice, we will consider how classroom practices can enable all children to make use of and further develop their plurilingual repertoires.
Session 7: Understanding Plurilingual and Pluricultural Experiences through the Narratives of “Children across Borders”
By reading essays and other writings by individuals who have experienced life as children across borders, we will examine plurilingual and pluricultural competence, Translanguaging practices, and identity.

Building on "Literacies of Children in a Multilingual Context 1", this course examines approaches to educational practice for "children across borders" through close reading of assigned texts, engagement in language activities, and the collaborative development of lesson plans and teaching/learning materials.　In particular, the course focuses on Translanguaging pedagogy that draws on children’s plurilingual repertoires, knowledge, and linguistic resources in order to further develop their plurilingual and pluricultural competence. Students will collaboratively create Translanguaging-based teaching and learning materials and educational practice plans that foster plurilingual literacy by making use of their own linguistic resources. The completed materials and practice plans will be published online* so that children growing up in multilingual contexts around the world, as well as their supporters, may freely access and use them.
*“Fukufuku (Plurilingual and Pluricultural) Literacy”
https://fukufukuliteracy.w.waseda.jp/
The lectures will be conducted primarily in Japanese; however, depending on students’ needs, English may also be used. In individual and group activities, students are encouraged to draw on their full linguistic repertoires to think, investigate, express ideas, and interact, thereby deepening their understanding of the issues under discussion and fostering mutual understanding among group members. Students with diverse linguistic backgrounds are welcome.
This course is open to both undergraduate and graduate students. While both groups attend the same in-person classes, they are assigned different coursework outside class. Undergraduate students will read assigned reference materials before class. After each session, undergraduate students will write a short reflection in response to questions presented in class and submit it via Moodle (approximately 30 minutes). The reflection should be approximately 500 Japanese characters or 250 words in English. Graduate students will read assigned readings and submit a written commentary via Moodle (approximately 1–2 hours). The commentary should be approximately 800 Japanese characters or 400–450 words in English. In their commentary, students are expected to address points of interest, questions, and issues for discussion. They will also provide comments on points raised by others.
All sessions of this course will be conducted in person in a classroom setting.
Because this course presupposes the theories and discussions covered in "Literacies of children in a multilingual context 1", Students are expected to take "Literacies of Children in a Multilingual Context 1" prior to or in sequence with this course.

Session 1: Educational Initiatives for Minority Languages — The Family Context
Through multiple case studies, we will examine how families support “children across borders” in learning minority languages that differ from those used in school and wider society. We will also explore the challenges, difficulties, tensions, strategies, richness, and enjoyment involved in minority language education in the home.
Session 2: Educational Initiatives for Minority Languages — The Community Context
Through case studies, we will examine how language communities support minority language education. We will consider the challenges and possibilities involved in creating spaces for language education within community settings.
Session 3: What Educational Practices Draw on and Develop All of Children’s Languages? — Translanguaging Theory and Practice
Through an introduction to Translanguaging theory and examples of educational practice, we will examine how classroom practices can draw on and further develop the plurilingual resources of all children.
Session 4: Examining and Experiencing Translanguaging in Practice
After reviewing examples of educational practices based on Translanguaging theory, students will engage in similar language activities by drawing on their own linguistic resources. Through reflection on these experiences, we will consider key perspectives and points of attention necessary for Translanguaging pedagogy.
Session 5: Designing Translanguaging Educational Practice Plans for “Children across Borders”
In groups, students will design Translanguaging-based educational practice plans tailored to the imagined backgrounds and subject areas of specific groups of children across borders.
Session 6: Developing Translanguaging Teaching and Learning Materials for “Children across Borders”
Individually or in groups, students will develop Translanguaging-based teaching and learning materials tailored to the imagined backgrounds of specific groups of children. In doing so, they will collaboratively draw on their own plurilingual resources.
Session 7: Presentation and Discussion of Translanguaging Practice Plans and Materials
Students will present the Translanguaging-based practice plans and materials developed in Sessions 5 and 6 and engage in peer discussion and feedback.

summary_excerpt: Responsible conduct of academic research entails not only ensuring integri......
summary:
Responsible conduct of academic research entails not only ensuring integrity in academia but also entailing responsibility for the people, the society, and the future through the research activity. However, this is not solely determined externally by laws, regulations, or social norms. It varies depending on the individual researcher's context and awareness, and must be continually revised as research activities progress. Precisely because scientific endeavors inherently possess various types of incertitude, it is difficult to consistently engage in actions that clearly define a subject and object of “responsibility.” Therefore, in this course, through group discussions we first share each student's concerns and understanding of what constitutes responsible academic research. Next, in lectures, we re-examine the inherent incertitude of academia itself from the perspectives of science, research, organizations, and society, opening discussions on how the relevant actors fulfill their social responsibilities within this framework. We then examine ethical issues that may arise in research activities through fictive case studies, identifying the diversity and commonalities in each student's understanding, and derive theoretical and practical implications for making responsible research activities more creative.
This course is intended for students who have taken the course “Introduction to Academic and Research Integrity”. Building upon the content covered in the Introduction, I would like students to discuss points that have caught their attention or topics they wish to explore further. Those who have taken the Introduction in previous years are also welcome.
This course will hold the first and last two sessions in the classroom, with the three sessions in between conducted as on-demand streaming lectures.
goal:
Graduate students aspiring to become researchers show their sense of ownership in responsible conduct of research and deepen their understanding of what constitutes such practices through discussion. Specific learning objectives are as follows:
• Explain the aspects of academic and research integrity that interest you most and the reasons why.
• Relate responsible conduct of research to your own research activities and share your understanding and concerns with fellow students.
• Appropriately understand and explain the relationship between incertitude in science and social responsibility.
• Infer appropriate actions to take from the perspective and role of parties involved when examining fictive cases related to responsible research activities, and devise various challenges and solutions.
• Relatively position your own understanding of responsible research activities and become aware of biases and dynamics in perception.
• Understand and respect the rules of dialogue in group work and engage in dialogue with others.

Read the assigned textbook and reading materials in advance (3 hours).
Prioritisation of the statement on responsible conduct of academic research (1 hour)
Implementation of tasks based on a fictive case study (5 hours)
schedule_plan:
1:
1. Personal Reflection on Responsible Conduct of Academic Research
After briefly reviewing the course “Introduction to Academic and Research Integrity” and confirming this course's objectives and approach, participants discuss the aspects they find most interesting and why. They also relate responsible research practices to their own research activities, sharing their understanding and concerns with fellow participants.
2:
2. Re-examining What Constitutes Responsible Conduct of Academic Research
After confirming each participant's understanding and concerns, they exchanging brief written statements on responsible conduct of academic research they deem important via group work. The group then collectively organise and refine these statements. By Session 6, participants are required to prioritize these statements.
3:
3. Incertitude of Science and Social Responsibility (1)
This session examines research as an act of advancing science, delving into the inevitable interaction between researchers and their subjects, as well as the tacit knowledge, serendipity, and normative aspects inherent in research. It then explores the incertitude of knowledge within organizational contexts such as laboratories, team science, and academic societies, and the social responsibility within them. Finally, it focuses on the evaluation process for confirming knowledge about research outcomes, clarifying the challenges arising from the correlation between research and evaluation at the individual, organizational, and systemic levels.
4:
4. Incertitude of Science and Social Responsibility (2)
We trace how knowledge generated by research has been utilised in industry and policy, exploring the responsibilities and governance models emerging with the advent of bidirectional knowledge flows between researchers and practitioners, exemplified by transdisciplinary research. Subsequently, we discuss academic issues in the context of societal digitalisation and globalisation, linking them to individual intellectual attitudes and awareness of responsibility. Finally, we look ahead to academia about the future and the future of academia itself, pursuing the transformation of concepts of publicness and responsibility through the involvement of a wide range of actors.
5:
5. Examination of Fictive Cases
We learn about the Seven-Step Guide as a method for ethical decision-making and use fictive cases to delve into specific points for consideration and challenges in ethical decision-making.
6:
6. Case Study Exercise
Using the fictive case, we practice the ethical decision-making process learned in Session 5. Participants will engage in role-playing to understand the perspectives and roles of each character in the case, discussing how to conduct more sincere and responsible research activities.
7:
7. Towards Creative Research Activities
We identify both the diversity and commonalities in each participant's perceptions based on the results of the prioritization of the statements created in Session 2. After participants recognise their own cognitive biases and cherished values, they understand the knowledge and skills necessary for academic research activities, whether conducted individually or organizationally, to be both sincere and creative. Finally, we will summarise this course, and each participant engage in reflection.

summary:
Design thinking is a well-known ideation method based on a human-centered approach, making it a powerful tool for solving complex problems. Addressing societal challenges requires balancing a deep understanding of individuals with a broader perspective while considering multiple stakeholders and influencing factors. Additionally, it is essential to make clear decisions despite incomplete information and to identify and select the most effective interventions from numerous possibilities. Human-Centered Design is recognized as both a robust methodology and a mindset for tackling such challenges.
This course aims to introduce the fundamental concepts of design thinking, fostering creativity and providing new perspectives on problem-solving. Design thinking is a highly versatile approach applicable to business, technology, art, and everyday life, offering a flexible and effective framework for addressing unknown challenges. Students will work on design challenges with randomly assigned teammates and engage in lectures, discussions, group work, fieldwork, and individual and group reflections to deepen their learning and develop practical skills.

summary:
本演習では，実社会におけるデジタルツインの活用事例を分析することを通じて，意思決定支援システムとしてのデジタルツインの特徴や設計上の考え方を学びます．エネルギー，交通，都市，地域などの社会システムを対象としたケーススタディを取り上げ，デジタルツインがどのような課題を対象とし，どのような情報を活用し，どのような意思決定を支援しているのかを読み解くことを目的とします．
また，各事例について，対象システムの特徴，利用されているデータやモデル，評価指標，制約条件，制度的背景などを整理し，設計上の工夫や限界について考察します．複数の事例を比較・分析することで，分野を超えて共通する設計思想や，社会課題に応じて異なる設計上の考え方を理解します．
本講義では，ケーススタディを分析する力を養うことに重点を置きます。実際にデジタルツインを設計・提案する演習については，後続の「デジタルツインに基づく意思決定演習２」で取り組みます．
goal:
- 社会課題に応じたデジタルツインの設計プロセスを説明できる．
- クライメイトポジティブ社会の実現に向けた文理融合・産学連携研究への活用事例を知る.
- 活用事例を分析し，設計思想や設計上の工夫を説明できる．
- 異なる分野の事例を比較し，共通する設計思想を説明できる．
study_outside: 授業テーマに関する講義資料に基づく１時間程度の概要予習と講義内容に関する１時間程度の復習を要する．

デジタルツインの活用事例を概観し，ケーススタディの分析方法と着眼点を整理する．
2:
第２回：エネルギーシステムにおける意思決定支援
エネルギー分野の事例を通じて，デジタルツインによる予測・運用・意思決定支援の仕組みを理解する．
3:
第３回：モビリティ・交通システムにおける意思決定支援
モビリティや交通システムにおけるデジタルツインの活用事例を分析し，設計上の特徴を理解する．
4:
第４回：都市システムにおける意思決定支援
都市運営や都市サービスを対象としたデジタルツインの活用事例を分析する．
5:
第５回：地域システムにおける意思決定支援
地域システムやレジリエンス分野におけるデジタルツインの役割と意思決定支援について理解する．
6:
第６回：分野横断型デジタルツインと文理融合・産学連携
異なる分野の事例を比較し，文理融合・産学連携による価値創造について考察する．
7:
第７回：ケーススタディの比較分析と設計思想の整理
各事例を比較し，デジタルツイン設計に共通する考え方と設計思想を整理する．

summary:
本演習では，実社会の課題を対象として，デジタルツインによる意思決定支援システムの構想・設計に取り組みます．特に「デジタルツインに基づく意思決定演習１」で学んだケーススタディの分析結果を踏まえ，社会課題に対するデジタルツインを自ら設計・提案する演習に取り組みます．対象システムの課題を整理し，必要なデータ，モデル，評価指標，制約条件などを検討しながら，意思決定支援システムとしてのデジタルツインを構想することを目的とします．
また，不確実性や説明可能性，制度的条件，社会受容性なども考慮しながら，実社会で活用可能なデジタルツインの設計について検討します．設計した内容は発表・討論を通じて相互に評価し，設計思想や改善点について議論することで，より実践的な理解を深めます．

- 社会課題に応じたデジタルツインを設計できる．
- クライメイトポジティブ社会の実現に向けたデジタルツインの活用方法を構想できる．
- 必要なデータ，モデル，評価指標，制約条件を整理できる．
- 小規模な設計課題を通じて意思決定支援のためのデジタルツインを提案できる．

summary:
■授業の目的
本授業の目的は、学術的文章の作成を指導する者を育成することです（全
14
回、対面授業です）。具体的には、
早稲田大学グローバル・エデュケーション・センターのアカデミック・ライティング教育部門
における、
学部生向け授業
の「指導員」（非対面、個別指導）、または学生・教員が利用する
ライティング・センター
における「チューター」（原則対面、個別指導）の候補者を育成します。そのために、本授業の履修者は、学術的文章の作成に必要な文章技術を身につけることを目標に学習します。
授業では、複数の文章技術を学びます。これから書く様々な文章において、どの文章技術を意識し、また組み合わせて使うとよいかを判断する基礎となる力を磨きます。
※履修後に「指導員」または「チューター」として勤務する気持ちのない方は、履修しないでください。
■授業の流れ
文章を書く技能は、他の技能と同様、文章へのフィードバックを受けて初めて磨かれるものです。しかし、文章へのフィードバックは、残念ながら、通常ではなかなか得ることができません。そこでこの授業では、論理的で明快な学術的文章を書くための文章技術を、実際に文章を書き、フィードバックを受け、直していくことで学びます。
具体的には、週ごとに一つの文章技術または一つのライティング・プロセスを学びます。毎回、クラスの他の履修者と文章を読み合い、ディスカッションをします。授業後に、その週の文章技術を使って課題文章を作成し、提出します。翌週の授業冒頭で、教員からのコメントが付いた課題文章が返却されます。毎回、返却された課題文章
1
、
2
編をクラスで共有し、ディスカッションします。活発な授業への参加を期待しています。

2

1
」と「
2
」の両方を、同時に履修登録してください。「
1
」のみ、または「
2
」のみの履修は認めません。

自らの商品アイデアや研究成果の技術を基にビジネスモデルを構築し，仮説検証を繰り返しながらそれをブラッシュアップすることで，事業をゼロから開発する手法を実践的に学ぶ．具体的には，事業開発の国際標準規格『ISO56002』で全体プロセスを把握し、そのプロセスに従って、事業開発の中核理論『ジョブ理論』、アイデアの発案手法である『デザイン思考』や『ビジネスモデル・キャンバス』、ビジネスモデルの検証手法である『リーンスタートアップ』や『顧客開発モデル』、収益性検証のための『シンプル収益モデル』などの事業開発手法を学習する。プロセスと手法を理解したら、実際に商品アイデアやビジネスモデルを発案し、顧客インタビューやプロトタイプ作成を通じてビジネスモデルの仮説検証を実践して力をつける．最終的には仮説検証の結果をすべて総括したビジネスプランを作成して、ビジネスコンテストさながらのピッチを行う.

「ビジネスモデル仮説検証の授業を受けて、これまで曖昧だった知識が明確になった気がする。なんとなく、「課題って大切だよなー」「ニーズはあった方がいいよなー」と考えていたが、ジョブ、課題、現状対策、残課題というニーズのメカニズムを常に意識して考えられるようになった。他にも、アーリーアダプターやインタビューなど、初めて学ぶことも多く、この授業によって知識的な土台ができた気がする。いろんな場面で自信を持って考えたり自分の意見を言ったりできるようになれそうだ。また、アプリを開発するときのアイデア出しにもどんどんこの授業で身につけたことを使っていきたい。」
「なんだかんだいちばん大事なのは、やっぱりチームメンバーだなと思いました。僕らのグループは非常にバランスもよく、各々が結構強みを活かせていたのかなという気がします。もちろん、インタビューもっとやろうと思えばできたなーとか、ここ追い込めればもっと良いもの作れたかもしれないと思う気持ちは多少残るし、チームメンバーにも迷惑をかけることも何回か合ったので、すごく申し訳ない気持ちもありました。それでもお互いにリスペクトして、がんばれたのは非常に良い経験だったなと個人的には思っています。」
「
起業のシード期における必要な流れを体型的に学ぶことができた。ビジネスを立ち上げるために必要な事項を丁寧に学ぶことができた。これまで、ビジネスモデルを構築するにあたって、何も知識がなかったため、とてもハードルが高く感じていた。しかし、授業を受けることによって、行わなければならないことが見えてきた。そのためハードルが低くなったように感じることができて良かった。」
「ビジネスモデルの組み立て方については抽象的には把握していたものの実際にビジネスコンテストに参加してみると不備ばかりで自分でもなかなか納得の行くプレゼンが作れていない状況でした。しかし、本講義を受講し、どのようにビジネスアイディアを創造し、仮説検証を行い、そして実際にマネタイズやスケーリングを考えるまでの一連の流れが身につきました。」
「ビジネスを実際に行うまでのイメージが具体的に分かりました。アットホームな雰囲気で色々な人達の意見を聞けます。初めて会う人とプランを考えるので自分にはない考えを発見できます。色々なアイデアを聞いて知らない事業機会も発見できました。」

name: Fundamentals and Practice of Business Idea Pitching
teacher: 莉々　紀子
summary_excerpt: This intensive course is designed to help students develop practical skill......
subtitle: From Concept to Global Presentation
summary: This intensive course is designed to help students develop practical skills to structure and deliver business ideas effectively in English within an international context. Conducted entirely in English, the course guides students through the entire process—from idea generation and opportunity recognition to storytelling, pitch deck creation, and delivery skills—using real cases from global startups and international pitch events. In the final session, students will present their own business ideas in English, simulating a global-standard pitch environment.
goal:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
1. Structure business ideas logically and present them clearly and persuasively to an international audience.
2. Acquire effective presentation skills in English, including storytelling and expressions required for pitching.
3. Understand and apply the structure, conventions, and expectations of pitches in global business contexts.
4. Demonstrate flexible communication skills for impromptu Q&A sessions and practice persuasive techniques tailored to the audience.
study_outside:
Preparation: Watch assigned materials such as TED Talks and international startup pitch videos, analyze expressions and structures, and prepare short summaries or opinions in English. Conduct research on a business idea related to one’s own field of interest and create notes in English.
Review: Revise pitch decks and scripts based on in-class feedback. Reflect on key takeaways from each session and prepare for the following class.
schedule_plan:
1:
Introduction, Global Pitching Landscape, and Key Principles (Fourth period, 10/06)
Course objectives, characteristics of international business pitching, case studies of global pitch competitions, key elements of globally effective pitches, and basic exercises in clear English expressions.
2:
From Idea to Opportunity & Finding and Shaping Ideas (Fifth period, 10/06)
Idea generation, identifying market needs, developing solutions from problems, group sharing of ideas, and impromptu speech practice.
3:
Business Model & Value Proposition for a Global Audience (Fourth period, 10/13)
Designing business models for international markets, articulating customer value in English, and practicing short speeches/mini-pitches.
4:
Storytelling, Pitch Structure, and Cross-Cultural Persuasion (Fifth period, 10/13)
Storytelling that resonates with global audiences, typical pitch structures (problem → solution → market → strengths), persuasive techniques across cultures, and hands-on exercises.
5:
Pitch Deck Design, Visual Communication, and Workshop (Fourth period, 10/20)
Creating effective slides, designing visual messages, explaining slides in English, analyzing sample pitch decks, and peer review of students’ own decks.
6:
Rehearsal, Mock Pitch, and Feedback Session (Fifth period, 10/20)
Group rehearsals, mock pitch sessions, immediate peer and instructor feedback, and identification of improvement points.
7:
Final Pitch Presentation (Fourth period, 10/27)
Students' final English business idea pitches, Q&A, and course wrap-up.
textbook: Course materials will be provided by the instructor.
reference:
Guy Kawasaki, The Art of the Start 2.0 (Portfolio, 2015)
Bill Aulet, Disciplined Entrepreneurship (Wiley, 2013)
John Doerr, Measure What Matters (Portfolio, 2017)
Archived videos of international pitch events (e.g., TechCrunch Disrupt, Slush, SXSW Pitch)
Supplementary materials: TED Talks on entrepreneurship, startup pitch videos, instructor-distributed materials, and online case studies
grading_method:
Class participation (active contribution in discussions and exercises) and review sheets: 30%
Assignments (idea summaries, short English presentations, etc.): 30%
Final pitch presentation: 40%
notes_url:
All sessions will be conducted in English.
No prior business experience or specific English proficiency level is required; however, active participation and willingness to take on challenges in a global, practice-oriented environment will be highly valued.
